papers.title: Evaluation of Adversarial Robustness in Arabic Language Models
papers.abstract: The emergence of the recent outstanding capabilities of Arabic Language Models has opened doors for exposing their vulnerabilities. One of the major security risks associated with such Natural Language Processing models is adversarial attacks. These attacks can deceive the model into the wrong prediction, raising critical model security and safety concerns. This study aims to assess the robustness of five state-of-the-art Arabic Language Models under a distinct set of Arabic adversarial attacks applied at various levels of granularity and using different example generation strategies. We also explore a defense technique based on adversarial training to enhance model robustness. The results show that insertion of diacritics can reduce the accuracy of some models by 92% while maintaining a low perturbation distance. For word-level attacks, manipulating Arabic conjunctions preserves high semantic similarity scores, low perturbation distance, and leads to an accuracy degradation of up to 58%. For sentence-level attacks, paraphrasing proves its effectiveness by an average reduction of 76% in the victim models' performance. While adversarial training improves overall resilience, with MARBERT being the most robust and AraBERT showing the greatest relative gains, challenges persist, particularly against character-level noise. These findings highlight both the potential and limitations of current defense strategies in morphologically rich languages like Arabic.

summary.takeaway: Adversarial attacks significantly degrade the performance of state-of-the-art Arabic language models, with character-level diacritics insertion causing up to 92% accuracy reduction, while adversarial training improves robustness but challenges remain.
summary.problem: Arabic language models are vulnerable to adversarial attacks at multiple granularity levels, threatening model security and reliability in critical applications.
summary.method: The study evaluates five Arabic language models under character-, word-, and sentence-level adversarial attacks and applies adversarial training as a defense mechanism.
summary.evidence: Insertion of diacritics reduced accuracy by up to 92%, word-level conjunction manipulations caused up to 58% degradation, and paraphrasing led to an average 76% performance drop; adversarial training improved resilience notably for MARBERT and AraBERT.
summary.limitations: Defense strategies remain less effective against character-level noise, and the study does not fully resolve robustness challenges in morphologically rich Arabic.
summary.why_for_you: This paper provides empirical insights into adversarial vulnerabilities and defense efficacy in Arabic LMs, informing efficient adversarial training and robustness evaluation in morphologically complex languages.

signals.text: Insertion of Arabic diacritics as a character-level attack reduces AraBERT accuracy by 92%, demonstrating extreme vulnerability to subtle orthographic perturbations.
Adversarial training using white-box gradient-based attacks under DistilBERT similarity constraints enhances robustness, with MARBERT showing the highest post-defense accuracy.

Perturbation rates measured by Levenshtein distance and semantic similarity via Universal Sentence Encoder confirm that attacks maintain high semantic similarity while significantly degrading model accuracy.

deep_dive.overview: This research investigates the adversarial robustness of five leading Arabic language models—MARBERT, AraBERT, CaMeLBERT, XLM-T, and mBERT—against attacks at character, word, and sentence levels. The study applies various adversarial example generation strategies, including diacritics insertion, conjunction manipulation, and paraphrasing, to evaluate model vulnerabilities. Character-level diacritics insertion causes the most severe accuracy drops, up to 92%, highlighting the sensitivity of Arabic LMs to orthographic noise. Word-level attacks that manipulate conjunctions preserve semantic similarity but degrade accuracy by up to 58%. Sentence-level paraphrasing reduces performance by an average of 76%. To mitigate these vulnerabilities, the authors implement adversarial training using gradient-based white-box attacks constrained by DistilBERT similarity, which improves robustness, especially for MARBERT and AraBERT. However, challenges persist, particularly against character-level noise, underscoring the complexity of defending morphologically rich languages like Arabic. The study employs quantitative metrics such as attack success rate, perturbation rate via Levenshtein distance, and semantic similarity measures to rigorously assess attack impact and defense efficacy.

methodology.title: Adversarial Attack Taxonomy and Generation
methodology.detail: Attacks are categorized by granularity: character-level (insertions, deletions, substitutions), word/token-level (synonym replacements, grammatical violations), and sentence-level (paraphrasing, substitutions). Example generation strategies include edit-based and importance-based methods, with importance-based attacks leveraging SHAP and Word Importance Rank to identify critical tokens for perturbation.

methodology.title: Adversarial Training Defense
methodology.detail: A vanilla adversarial training approach (A2T) is applied, generating white-box gradient-based attacks constrained by DistilBERT similarity to augment training data. This method aims to reduce computational complexity and improve model resilience by exposing models to adversarial examples during training.

methodology.title: Evaluation Metrics
methodology.detail: Attack success rate (ASR) measures the proportion of adversarial examples causing misclassification. Perturbation rate is quantified using Levenshtein distance to capture edit operations between original and perturbed inputs. Semantic similarity is assessed via cosine similarity and Universal Sentence Encoder (USE) scores to ensure adversarial examples preserve meaning.

methodology.title: Model Selection and Baselines
methodology.detail: Five state-of-the-art Arabic language models—MARBERT, AraBERT, CaMeLBERT, XLM-T, and mBERT—are evaluated. Baseline accuracies on clean test sets range from 87% (mBERT) to 99% (MARBERT), providing a reference for assessing adversarial impact.

mechanism.title: No Explicit Mechanism Provided
mechanism.detail: The paper does not present formal equations or causal mechanisms explaining adversarial vulnerability or defense efficacy beyond empirical evaluation metrics and attack taxonomies.

experiments.title: Character-Level Diacritics Insertion Attack
experiments.detail: Diacritics are inserted into Arabic text inputs to create adversarial examples. Models are evaluated on accuracy degradation, perturbation rate (Levenshtein distance), and semantic similarity (USE). MARBERT shows 94% post-attack accuracy, while AraBERT accuracy drops by 92%.

experiments.title: Word-Level Conjunction Manipulation Attack
experiments.detail: Attacks manipulate Arabic conjunctions to preserve semantic similarity and low perturbation distance. This leads to accuracy degradation up to 58% across victim models, demonstrating effective word-level adversarial strategies.

experiments.title: Sentence-Level Paraphrasing Attack
experiments.detail: Paraphrasing techniques generate sentence-level adversarial examples, causing an average 76% reduction in model performance, highlighting the potency of semantic-level perturbations.

experiments.title: Adversarial Training Evaluation
experiments.detail: Models undergo adversarial training using gradient-based white-box attacks with DistilBERT similarity constraints. Post-training evaluations show improved robustness, with MARBERT being the most resilient and AraBERT exhibiting the largest relative gains.

findings.title: Extreme Vulnerability to Diacritics Insertion
findings.detail: Insertion of diacritics reduces AraBERT accuracy by 92% and CaMeLBERT by 80%, while MARBERT maintains 94% accuracy, indicating model-specific robustness differences.

findings.title: Word-Level Attacks Preserve Semantics but Reduce Accuracy
findings.detail: Manipulating Arabic conjunctions maintains high semantic similarity and low perturbation distance but causes up to 58% accuracy degradation, confirming the effectiveness of word-level adversarial attacks.

findings.title: Sentence-Level Paraphrasing Severely Impacts Performance
findings.detail: Paraphrasing attacks reduce victim model performance by an average of 76%, demonstrating the potency of sentence-level adversarial perturbations.

findings.title: Adversarial Training Enhances Robustness
findings.detail: Adversarial training improves overall resilience, with MARBERT showing the highest robustness and AraBERT achieving the greatest relative improvement, though challenges remain against character-level noise.

findings.title: Semantic Similarity Maintained in Adversarial Examples
findings.detail: High cosine similarity and USE scores indicate that adversarial examples preserve semantic content despite causing significant accuracy drops.

contributions: Comprehensive evaluation of five state-of-the-art Arabic language models under multi-granularity adversarial attacks.
Demonstration of severe vulnerability of Arabic LMs to character-level diacritics insertion attacks.
Application and assessment of adversarial training defense improving robustness, especially for MARBERT and AraBERT.
Use of semantic similarity metrics alongside perturbation measures to validate adversarial example quality.
Highlighting persistent challenges in defending morphologically rich languages like Arabic against character-level noise.
limitations: Defense strategies remain less effective against character-level noise such as diacritics insertion.
The study does not explore multi-level or combined adversarial attacks in depth.
Limited discussion on the computational cost and scalability of adversarial training for large Arabic LMs.
No formal mechanistic explanation or theoretical modeling of adversarial vulnerabilities is provided.
open_questions: How can defense mechanisms be improved to effectively counter character-level adversarial noise in morphologically rich languages?
What are the trade-offs between robustness and computational efficiency in adversarial training for Arabic LMs?
Can multi-level adversarial attacks combining character, word, and sentence perturbations reveal new vulnerabilities?
How do dialectal variations in Arabic affect adversarial robustness and defense strategies?

papers.title: On-Policy Distillation for LLM Safety: A Routing Approach to Template-Robust Realignment
papers.abstract: Fine-tuning is the dominant paradigm for specializing large language models (LLMs), yet it exposes a critical vulnerability: malicious data providers can embed harmful behaviors into downstream corpora, creating models that retain professional skills while violating human values on demand. Existing safety-realignment defenses often fail in practice due to three key limitations: they frequently cause catastrophic forgetting of specialized skills; their effectiveness collapses when the defender cannot observe the attacker's prompt template; and successfully realigned models remain susceptible to re-jailbreaking via simple system prompt switches. To address these challenges, we propose Routing-based On-Policy Distillation (ROPD), a novel realignment framework that models the divergence between aligned and compromised output probability distributions rather than fitting specific prompt templates. We conduct extensive experiments comparing ROPD against four state-of-the-art baselines across three datasets and three base models with varying alignment strengths. Our results demonstrate that when baseline defenses face template mismatches, often accompanied by severe degradation in downstream task performance. In contrast, ROPD substantially mitigates template-mismatch risks, maintaining superior robustness in both defense effectiveness and capability preservation. While our analysis indicates ROPD is not entirely immune to template shifts, its performance degradation is negligible compared to existing methods, establishing a new standard for robust LLM realignment.

summary.takeaway: Routing-based On-Policy Distillation (ROPD) effectively mitigates template-mismatch vulnerabilities in LLM safety realignment.
summary.problem: Existing safety-realignment defenses often fail due to catastrophic forgetting, template dependency, and susceptibility to re-jailbreaking.
summary.method: ROPD models the divergence between aligned and compromised output distributions, using a dual-teacher framework for realignment.
summary.evidence: ROPD outperforms four state-of-the-art baselines, maintaining task performance while reducing harmful output rates significantly.
summary.limitations: ROPD is not entirely immune to template shifts, experiencing some performance degradation under certain conditions.
summary.why_for_you: This research provides a novel approach to enhance LLM safety, relevant for developing robust AI systems.

signals.text: ROPD maintains superior robustness against template mismatches, achieving a reduction in harmful output rates (ASR) to single-digit levels while preserving task performance.
The dual-teacher configuration in ROPD utilizes a safety teacher for refusal behavior and a task teacher for downstream capabilities, effectively routing realignment tokens.
Baseline methods showed over 30% degradation in defense effectiveness when faced with template mismatches, while ROPD's performance degradation was negligible.

deep_dive.overview: This paper addresses the vulnerabilities of existing safety-realignment methods for large language models (LLMs), which often fail due to catastrophic forgetting and template dependency. The authors propose Routing-based On-Policy Distillation (ROPD), a novel framework that models the divergence between aligned and compromised output distributions. Extensive experiments demonstrate that ROPD significantly mitigates template-mismatch risks, outperforming four state-of-the-art baselines across three datasets and models, while preserving downstream task performance.

methodology.title: ROPD Framework
methodology.detail: ROPD employs a dual-teacher setup where one teacher provides a refusal prior and the other maintains task capabilities. The model routes tokens based on their source, optimizing with a top-K KL divergence objective.

methodology.title: Training Procedure
methodology.detail: The training involves a mixture of task and harmful data, with the model initialized from a misaligned state. The training objective focuses on minimizing the divergence between the student model's outputs and the teachers' outputs.

methodology.title: Evaluation Protocol
methodology.detail: The evaluation measures the attack success rate (ASR) across different templates, assessing the robustness of ROPD against template shifts compared to baseline methods.

mechanism.title: Output Probability Distillation
mechanism.detail: ROPD distills the output distribution of the aligned model, focusing on refusal behaviors that are less dependent on specific prompt templates, thereby enhancing robustness.

experiments.title: Baseline Comparisons
experiments.detail: ROPD was compared against SSRD, RESTA, soft-SFT, and rollback across three datasets (text-to-SQL, dialogue summarization, NL2Bash) and three models (Llama-2, Qwen2.5, Gemma2), demonstrating superior performance.

experiments.title: Template Mismatch Evaluation
experiments.detail: Experiments showed that baseline defenses suffered over 30% performance degradation under template mismatches, while ROPD maintained effectiveness with minimal degradation.

findings.title: Defense Effectiveness
findings.detail: ROPD achieved a low ASR of 1.6% under the self-defense template, significantly outperforming baselines that had ASRs above 30%.

findings.title: Task Performance Preservation
findings.detail: ROPD maintained or improved task performance across all evaluated models, contrasting with baselines that often resulted in zero task performance.

findings.title: Robustness Against Template Shifts
findings.detail: While ROPD is not immune to template shifts, its performance degradation is significantly lower than that of existing methods, establishing a new standard for LLM realignment.

contributions: Introduction of Routing-based On-Policy Distillation (ROPD) as a novel framework for LLM safety realignment.
Demonstration of ROPD's effectiveness in mitigating template-mismatch vulnerabilities.
Empirical validation of ROPD's robustness across multiple datasets and models.
limitations: ROPD is not entirely immune to template shifts, experiencing some performance degradation.
The framework's effectiveness is contingent on the quality of the teacher models used.
open_questions: How can ROPD be further improved to achieve complete immunity to template shifts?
What additional mechanisms can be integrated into ROPD to enhance its robustness against novel attack strategies?

papers.title: Language Models are not Equally Robust to Non-Canonical Tokenization across Languages
papers.abstract: Despite the existence of exponentially many valid tokenizations for a given string, language models operate on a single canonical sequence deterministically produced by the tokenizer, leaving the broader tokenization space largely uncharacterized. In this paper, we investigate this overlooked space by studying the behavior of language models under non-canonical tokenizations across diverse languages. For English, prior work shows that models are largely invariant to alternative tokenizations that represent the same underlying string. We ask whether this invariance generalizes to other languages beyond English. We conduct a multilingual study across 27 languages spanning diverse scripts and evaluate LLM behavior under alternative tokenizations across six downstream tasks. We find that tokenization invariance does not generalize: model behavior varies substantially across languages with instruction-tuned models exhibiting an average relative performance drop of 23.7% for Llama-3.1-8B, 11.4% for Qwen3-8B, and 9.9% for Gemma-3-12B. The variation of tokenization invariance is systematic across languages. Languages that exhibit higher token fragmentation show significantly greater sensitivity to non-canonical tokenizations. Our study of tokenization robustness serves as a diagnostic of how tightly a model is coupled to its tokenizer. These results demonstrate that tokenization robustness is not a universal property of language models, but depends strongly on the language and its interaction with the tokenizer. We also show that LoRA fine-tuning with multi-tokenization training data provides an effective mitigation for tokenization sensitivity. Fine-tuning on English alone improves tokenization robustness across languages, while systematically sampling diverse non-canonical tokenizations achieves the strongest overall performance.

summary.takeaway: Tokenization robustness varies significantly across languages and models, challenging the assumption of universal invariance.
summary.problem: The generalizability of tokenization invariance in language models beyond English is unclear.
summary.method: A multilingual study across 27 languages evaluated LLM behavior under non-canonical tokenizations across six downstream tasks.
summary.evidence: Instruction-tuned models showed average performance drops of 23.7% for Llama-3.1-8B, 11.4% for Qwen3-8B, and 9.9% for Gemma-3-12B under non-canonical tokenizations.
summary.limitations: The study does not explore the effects of non-canonical tokenization on all possible language families or scripts.
summary.why_for_you: Understanding tokenization robustness is crucial for improving multilingual LLM performance and addressing efficiency in adversarial training.

signals.text: Instruction-tuned models exhibit a systematic performance drop across languages when faced with non-canonical tokenizations, indicating that tokenization robustness is not universally applicable.
LoRA fine-tuning with multi-tokenization training data effectively mitigates tokenization sensitivity, enhancing robustness across languages.

Higher token fragmentation in certain languages correlates with increased sensitivity to non-canonical tokenizations, revealing a complex interaction between language characteristics and model performance.

deep_dive.overview: This research investigates the robustness of language models to non-canonical tokenizations across 27 languages, revealing that tokenization invariance observed in English does not extend universally. The study finds significant performance drops in instruction-tuned models, with an average decrease of 23.7% for Llama-3.1-8B, highlighting the influence of language-specific characteristics on model behavior. The findings suggest that tokenization robustness is a nuanced property shaped by the interaction between language and tokenizer, with implications for multilingual model training and evaluation.

methodology.title: Multilingual Study Design
methodology.detail: The study involved evaluating LLMs across 27 languages using six downstream tasks, focusing on how models respond to non-canonical tokenizations.

methodology.title: Performance Measurement
methodology.detail: Performance drops were quantified by comparing model outputs under canonical and non-canonical tokenizations, using metrics such as accuracy and task-specific benchmarks.

methodology.title: LoRA Fine-Tuning
methodology.detail: LoRA fine-tuning was applied using multi-tokenization training data to enhance model robustness, demonstrating improved performance across languages.

methodology.title: Token Fragmentation Analysis
methodology.detail: The average number of tokens per word was computed to assess token fragmentation, correlating it with model sensitivity to non-canonical tokenizations.

mechanism.title: Tokenization as a Latent Space
mechanism.detail: The study conceptualizes tokenization as a latent probabilistic space, where the variability in tokenization can influence model performance and robustness.

experiments.title: Model Evaluation Framework
experiments.detail: Experiments utilized the lm-evaluation-harness framework, extending it to support non-canonical tokenizations and character-level tokenizations for comprehensive evaluation.

experiments.title: Sampling Non-Canonical Tokenizations
experiments.detail: Random non-canonical tokenizations were generated using a Multi-valued Decision Diagram (MDD) to uniformly sample from the space of all valid tokenizations.

experiments.title: Instruction-Tuned Model Performance
experiments.detail: The main experiments focused on instruction-tuned models: Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen3-8B, and Gemma-3-12B, assessing their robustness across various languages.

findings.title: Performance Drop Across Languages
findings.detail: Instruction-tuned models experienced an average performance drop of 23.7% for Llama-3.1-8B, 11.4% for Qwen3-8B, and 9.9% for Gemma-3-12B under non-canonical tokenizations.

findings.title: Systematic Variation of Robustness
findings.detail: The study found that tokenization invariance varies systematically across languages, with higher token fragmentation leading to greater sensitivity.

findings.title: Mitigation through Fine-Tuning
findings.detail: LoRA fine-tuning with diverse non-canonical tokenizations improved robustness, demonstrating that training on English alone can enhance performance across languages.

contributions: First systematic study of non-canonical tokenization in multilingual LLMs across 27 languages and six tasks.
Analysis of how non-canonical tokenization affects multilingual models differently across language families and scripts.
Demonstration that non-canonical tokenization can serve as a natural source of data augmentation for improving multilingual generalization.
limitations: The study does not explore the effects of non-canonical tokenization on all possible language families or scripts.
Limited understanding of how tokenization robustness varies in lower-resource languages.
open_questions: How can tokenization robustness be improved for lower-resource languages?
What are the implications of tokenization variability for model safety and alignment in multilingual contexts?

papers.title: DataOrchestra: Learning to Orchestrate Per-Example Curation of Pretraining Data
papers.abstract: Pretraining data processing is critical to the downstream performance of Large Language Models (LLMs). However, many existing approaches define a fixed processing strategy at the corpus or domain level and apply it uniformly to many examples, without adapting to the needs of each example. We propose DataOrchestra, a framework that unifies different processing operations and orchestrates an example-specific pipeline for each example. Given a chunk of pretraining data, an orchestrator decides whether to drop, untouch, or clean it. For a chunk to be cleaned, it selects one or more downstream operations, ranging from programmatic editing to different forms of LLM-based rewriting. For each rewriting step, it further generates a concrete instruction, which is executed by the corresponding downstream tool model. We pretrain models from 0.5B to 7B from scratch on web data processed by DataOrchestra and observe stable average gains over individual data-processing methods across 11 benchmarks. DataOrchestra is also effective for math continued pretraining and outperforms stronger processing baselines, while reducing processing compute by skipping unnecessary downstream operations.

summary.takeaway: DataOrchestra adaptively orchestrates per-example pretraining data curation by deciding to drop, keep, or clean chunks with tailored downstream operations, improving LLM performance across benchmarks while reducing compute.
summary.problem: Existing pretraining data processing methods apply fixed, uniform strategies at corpus or domain level, failing to adapt to the diverse needs of individual data examples.
summary.method: DataOrchestra employs an orchestrator model that generates example-specific multi-stage plans involving noise pruning, surface rectification, and pedagogical augmentation, with fine-grained plan evolution and chunk-specific rewriting instructions executed by downstream tool models.
summary.evidence: Models pretrained from 0.5B to 7B parameters on DataOrchestra-processed web data show stable average gains over individual data-processing baselines across 11 benchmarks, including math continued pretraining, while reducing compute by skipping unnecessary operations.
summary.limitations: The paper does not provide explicit analysis of potential failure modes of the orchestrator under diverse data distributions or detailed cost-benefit tradeoffs of skipping operations beyond compute savings.
summary.why_for_you: DataOrchestra offers a novel, adaptive framework for per-example data selection and processing that can enhance LLM pretraining quality and efficiency, directly addressing challenges in data curation for large-scale language models.

signals.text: DataOrchestra’s orchestrator adaptively routes chunks to drop, untouch, or cleaning stages (noise pruning, surface rectification, pedagogical augmentation) based on a teacher LLM’s scoring and verifier LLM’s feedback, enabling example-specific processing.

The fine-grained plan evolution mechanism refines coarse-grained plans by verifying actual tool-model outputs, removing ineffective or harmful stages, and generating chunk-specific rewriting instructions to improve fidelity and reduce hallucination.

Empirical results show DataOrchestra outperforms strong baselines like ProX, RePro, and ReWire on 11 benchmarks, with gains increasing at larger model scales and consistent improvements across multiple web corpora and math continued pretraining.

deep_dive.overview: DataOrchestra addresses the limitation of fixed, uniform pretraining data processing by introducing an orchestrator that dynamically decides, for each data chunk, whether to drop it, leave it untouched, or clean it using a tailored pipeline of operations: noise pruning (NP), surface rectification (SR), and pedagogical augmentation (PA). The orchestrator is trained using a teacher LLM that scores chunks and proposes coarse plans, which are then refined through fine-grained plan evolution by verifier LLMs that assess the actual impact of cleaning stages on content fidelity and noise removal. This adaptive approach allows skipping unnecessary operations, saving compute while improving data quality. Experiments on models from 0.5B to 7B parameters pretrained on multiple web corpora demonstrate consistent average performance gains across 11 diverse benchmarks, including knowledge and language understanding tasks. DataOrchestra also excels in domain-specific continued pretraining for math, outperforming stronger baselines. The framework unifies multiple data-processing methods and adapts them per example, overcoming the limitations of prior fixed or uniform pipelines.

methodology.title: Orchestrator Training
methodology.detail: The orchestrator is trained on a curated pool of 160K documents sampled to balance low- and high-quality data, using a teacher LLM to assign scores and generate coarse-grained plans indicating drop, untouch, or cleaning stages (NP, SR, PA). The training objective is to learn to predict these plans for each chunk.

methodology.title: Fine-Grained Plan Evolution
methodology.detail: After generating coarse plans, the orchestrator refines them by executing selected cleaning stages with downstream tool models and verifying outputs with a verifier LLM. Stages that cause minimal or harmful changes (e.g., over-pruning or hallucination) are removed, and chunk-specific rewriting instructions are generated to guide downstream models.

methodology.title: Downstream Cleaning Operations
methodology.detail: Three cleaning operations are unified: noise pruning (programmatic line-level edits to remove ads and boilerplate), surface rectification (LLM rewriting to fix formatting and grammar), and pedagogical augmentation (LLM rewriting to add explanations and improve educational value). Each operation is applied adaptively per chunk.

methodology.title: Evaluation Protocol
methodology.detail: Models pretrained from scratch at scales 0.5B, 1.5B, and 7B parameters on DataOrchestra-processed data are evaluated on 11 benchmarks spanning knowledge and language understanding tasks. Metrics include accuracy averaged over three recent checkpoints to reduce variance.

mechanism.title: Adaptive Per-Example Pipeline Orchestration
mechanism.detail: DataOrchestra’s mechanism involves a multi-stage decision process: first, a teacher LLM scores each chunk for salvageable value and decides to drop or keep it; second, it predicts which cleaning stages are needed; third, a verifier LLM assesses the actual effect of each cleaning stage, removing ineffective ones and generating chunk-specific instructions. This feedback loop ensures that only beneficial operations are applied, optimizing data quality and compute.

experiments.title: Pretraining on Web Corpora
experiments.detail: Models from 0.5B to 7B parameters are pretrained from scratch on web data processed by DataOrchestra and compared against baselines including ProX, RePro, and ReWire. Evaluation is conducted on 11 benchmarks such as ARC, MMLU, HellaSwag, and RACE, reporting average accuracy over multiple checkpoints.

experiments.title: Generalization to Multiple Datasets
experiments.detail: DataOrchestra is applied to three additional web corpora (DCLM-RefinedWeb, C4, FineWeb) with 0.5B parameter models pretrained from scratch, showing consistent average gains over baselines, demonstrating robustness across data sources.

experiments.title: Math Continued Pretraining
experiments.detail: Using Davinci-Origin-3B as a base, DataOrchestra is applied for continued pretraining on math domain data, outperforming stronger processing baselines and improving domain-specific knowledge representation.

experiments.title: Ablation Studies
experiments.detail: Ablations removing fine-grained plan evolution or chunk-specific rewriting instructions show performance drops, confirming the importance of these components. Analysis of orchestrator decisions reveals sensible routing correlated with chunk quality scores.

findings.title: Performance Gains Across Scales
findings.detail: DataOrchestra achieves the highest average accuracy on 11 benchmarks at all model scales (0.5B, 1.5B, 7B), with the performance gap over baselines increasing with model size.

findings.title: Compute Efficiency
findings.detail: By skipping unnecessary cleaning stages for many chunks (about 35% dropped or left untouched initially), DataOrchestra reduces processing compute compared to uniform multi-stage pipelines.

findings.title: Effectiveness of Plan Evolution
findings.detail: Fine-grained plan evolution improves rewriting quality by removing stages that cause hallucination or minimal change, supported by verifier LLM assessments and ablation results showing performance degradation without evolution.

findings.title: Robustness Across Corpora
findings.detail: Consistent average gains on multiple web corpora indicate that DataOrchestra’s benefits are not corpus-specific but generalize across diverse data sources.

findings.title: Improved Domain Adaptation
findings.detail: In math continued pretraining, DataOrchestra outperforms stronger baselines, demonstrating its ability to adaptively curate domain-specific data for enhanced knowledge representation.

contributions: A unified framework (DataOrchestra) that adaptively orchestrates per-example pretraining data curation by integrating multiple cleaning operations.
A fine-grained plan evolution mechanism that refines coarse plans using verifier LLM feedback and generates chunk-specific rewriting instructions.
Demonstration of consistent performance improvements across model scales, benchmarks, and datasets, including domain-specific continued pretraining.
Empirical evidence that adaptive skipping of unnecessary operations reduces compute while improving data quality.
Open-source release of code enabling reproducibility and further research.
limitations: Lack of detailed analysis on orchestrator failure modes or robustness under highly diverse or adversarial data distributions.
Limited discussion on the tradeoffs between compute savings and potential missed improvements from skipped operations.
No explicit mechanism or theoretical model explaining the causal impact of each cleaning operation on downstream performance.
Evaluation focuses on accuracy metrics without extensive analysis of linguistic diversity or qualitative aspects of rewritten data.
open_questions: How does the orchestrator perform on data distributions with extreme noise or rare content types not seen during training?
Can the framework be extended to incorporate additional or more fine-grained cleaning operations beyond NP, SR, and PA?
What are the long-term effects of adaptive data curation on model generalization and robustness to out-of-distribution inputs?
How can the tradeoff between compute efficiency and maximal data quality improvement be optimally balanced in practice?

papers.title: When Derived Measurements Mislead: Quantifying and Mitigating LLM Over-Trust with Privileged-Modality Reliability Evidence
papers.abstract: Derived measurements increasingly enter large language model (LLM) pipelines as direct facts despite their instance-dependent validity. We define derived-feature over-trust (DFOT) as the failure in which a downstream LLM assigns such a measurement the epistemic status of a direct fact or uses it outside its valid scope. Using physiological sensing as a case study, D1 tests acceptance of a PPG-derived rhythm contradicted by offline ECG, whereas D2 tests rejection of an offline-confirmed reliable PPG rhythm under misleading severe history. ECG supplies training supervision and offline reference construction but is never shown to the LLM. Five estimands quantify this chain: conflict over-trust rate (COTR) and context-induced error rate (CIR) characterize D1/D2; correct repair rate (CRR) measures frozen-error repair; evidence-specific repair margin (ESRM) contrasts matched and patient-disjoint shuffled evidence; and utility harm rate (UHR) measures unnecessary verification among HIGH-reliability cases used without verification at baseline. The framework does not depend on a particular reliability generator. We demonstrate it on 50,000 paired PPG-ECG records using ECG-to-PPG privileged distillation as an illustrative baseline and PPG-only inference. On a protocol-locked 187-patient test, the baseline improves four repair and specificity endpoints by 1.82-6.69 percentage points, with all paired confidence intervals excluding zero; UHR increases by 0.67 percentage points (95% CI: -0.4 to +1.7). DFOT provides a common evaluation target for stronger mitigation methods. The code is available at https://github.com/Zongheng-Guo/When-Derived-Measurements-Mislead.

summary.takeaway: We demonstrate it on 50,000 paired PPG-ECG records using ECG-to-PPG privileged distillation as an illustrative baseline and PPG-only inference.
summary.problem: Derived measurements increasingly enter large language model (LLM) pipelines as direct facts despite their instance-dependent validity.
summary.method: The framework does not depend on a particular reliability generator.
summary.evidence: We demonstrate it on 50,000 paired PPG-ECG records using ECG-to-PPG privileged distillation as an illustrative baseline and PPG-only inference.
summary.limitations: The abstract does not state complete limitations; verify the experimental setup, baselines, and scope before relying on the result.
