papers.title: OptimismBench: Forecasting Bias and the Alignment Effect in Language Model Judgment
papers.abstract: Large language models are increasingly used as decision aids whose probability judgments shape downstream choices. Whether those judgments carry a systematic directional tilt has been hard to detect: calibration metrics aggregate unsigned errors, and naturalistic uncertainty offers no ground-truth probability. When an LLM rates a startup's success at 70% but its failure at 15%, the missing 15 points expose a distortion no aggregate score flags. We introduce OptimismBench, which detects directional bias with inverted pairs: each scenario elicits both P(success) and P(failure), and asymmetry between the two framings yields a signed bias score without ground truth. Across 16 models from 8 providers, fourteen are optimistic; pessimism appears only in Anthropic's frontier tier. Eleven matched base-versus-chat pairs across four families show post-training sets the sign of the bias, with opposite shifts in different families. The pattern survives prompt, temperature, perspective, and self-debiasing ablations. A seventeen-model six-language comparison further shows model identity dominates language, with inter-model variance at 4.7x inter-language variance. We release 3,870 items across 10 languages for per-model directional-bias auditing. When alignment makes a model more helpful, it also tilts its probabilities; downstream pipelines inherit the tilt by default.

summary.takeaway: OptimismBench reveals that most large language models exhibit a significant optimism bias in probability judgments, with alignment training influencing the direction and magnitude of this bias.
summary.problem: Existing calibration metrics fail to detect directional bias in LLM probability judgments, obscuring systematic optimism or pessimism in model outputs.
summary.method: OptimismBench uses inverted pairs eliciting complementary probabilities (P(success) and P(failure)) to compute a signed Skew score that quantifies directional bias without requiring ground-truth probabilities.
summary.evidence: Across 16 models from 8 providers and 10 languages, 14 models show significant optimism bias while only Anthropic’s frontier models show pessimism; this pattern persists under prompt, temperature, perspective, and self-debiasing variations.
summary.limitations: The family-direction claim is supported by limited matched pairs and single-pair pilots; Skew measures internal asymmetry rather than deviation from human judgment, lacking a matched human baseline.
summary.why_for_you: Understanding and auditing directional bias in LLM probability judgments is critical for trustworthy AI deployment, especially as alignment interventions can unintentionally amplify optimism bias affecting downstream decisions.

signals.text: The study finds that 14 out of 16 evaluated LLMs exhibit optimism bias with Skew scores ranging from +4.2 to +16.6, while only Anthropic’s frontier-tier models (Opus and Sonnet) show pessimism with Skew −5.1 and −7.7.

The inverted-pair method computes Skew as P(success) minus the complement of P(failure), enabling detection of directional bias without ground-truth probabilities by exploiting complementary probability elicitation.

Variance decomposition attributes 35.3% of Skew variance to model identity, 24.2% to scenario, and only 3.7% to domain, indicating that directional bias is primarily a model property rather than domain-dependent.

deep_dive.overview: This paper addresses the challenge of detecting directional bias in large language model (LLM) probability judgments, which traditional calibration metrics fail to reveal due to their aggregation of unsigned errors. The authors introduce OptimismBench, a novel benchmark leveraging inverted pairs of complementary probability queries (P(success) and P(failure)) to compute a signed Skew score that quantifies optimism or pessimism without requiring ground-truth probabilities. Evaluating 16 models from 8 providers across 60 scenarios and 10 languages, the study finds that most models exhibit significant optimism bias, except for Anthropic’s frontier models which show pessimism. The bias persists across prompt variations, temperature settings, perspective shifts, and explicit self-debiasing interventions. Controlled base-versus-chat comparisons reveal that post-training alignment strongly influences bias direction in a family-specific manner. Cross-lingual analysis shows model identity dominates language effects, with inter-model variance 4.7 times greater than inter-language variance. The benchmark and dataset are released for replication and auditing. These findings highlight a previously unmeasured alignment side-effect where increased helpfulness correlates with directional probability distortion, which downstream applications inherit by default.

methodology.title: Inverted-Pair Skew Scoring
methodology.detail: For each scenario, the model is prompted to estimate both P(success) and P(failure). The Skew score is computed as Skew = P(success) − (100 − P(failure)), capturing directional asymmetry in probability judgments without requiring ground-truth probabilities.

methodology.title: Base-versus-Chat Controlled Probe
methodology.detail: Eleven matched base-versus-chat model pairs across four families (Qwen, Llama, Gemma, Mistral) are evaluated to isolate the effect of post-training alignment on bias direction, holding architecture and pre-training constant.

methodology.title: Robustness Checks
methodology.detail: The study tests the stability of Skew under variations in system prompt detail (minimal, standard, extended), temperature (0.7 vs. 1.0), perspective (third-person, second-person, friend), and explicit self-debiasing prompts, confirming direction preservation.

methodology.title: Cross-Lingual Evaluation
methodology.detail: Seventeen models are evaluated across six native-prompt languages plus four with English system prompts, enabling variance decomposition that shows model identity dominates language effects on directional bias.

methodology.title: Probability Axiom Batteries
methodology.detail: Two probability coherence tests—conjunction (P(A) ≥ P(A ∩ B)) and dose-response monotonicity—are applied to five models, revealing low conjunction violation rates but high dose-response reversal rates, indicating differential alignment effects on coherence axioms.

mechanism.title: Directional Bias Measurement via Complementarity
mechanism.detail: The mechanism relies on the complementarity axiom of probabilities: a consistent model should produce P(success) and P(failure) estimates summing to 100%. Deviations from this complementarity, quantified by Skew, reveal directional bias. No explicit causal or geometric equations are provided.

experiments.title: 16-Model Directional Bias Evaluation
experiments.detail: Sixteen models from eight providers (OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Meta, Alibaba, DeepSeek, Mistral, Zhipu) are evaluated on 60 inverted-pair scenarios in 10 languages, measuring Skew scores and statistical significance (p < 0.002).

experiments.title: Base-versus-Chat Alignment Probe
experiments.detail: Eleven matched base-versus-chat pairs across four model families are tested to causally link post-training alignment to bias direction, showing family-specific shifts: Qwen alignment compresses bias, Llama alignment amplifies optimism.

experiments.title: Robustness Ablations
experiments.detail: Prompt detail, temperature, perspective, and self-debiasing interventions are ablated on selected models (e.g., GPT-5.4, Sonnet), confirming that directional bias sign remains stable with minor magnitude changes.

experiments.title: Cross-Lingual Variance Decomposition
experiments.detail: Seventeen models evaluated across six native languages plus four English-prompted languages show inter-model variance in Skew is 4.7 times greater than inter-language variance, emphasizing model identity as the dominant factor.

findings.title: Widespread Optimism Bias
findings.detail: Fourteen of sixteen models exhibit significant optimism bias with Skew scores from +4.2 to +16.6; only Anthropic’s frontier models (Opus −5.1, Sonnet −7.7) show pessimism, indicating optimism is the dominant directional bias.

findings.title: Alignment Influences Bias Direction
findings.detail: Post-training alignment causally sets bias direction in a family-specific manner: Qwen alignment reduces optimism bias, Llama alignment increases it, and Anthropic’s larger models shift from optimism to pessimism.

findings.title: Bias Persists Across Robustness Checks
findings.detail: Directional bias sign is preserved under variations in prompt detail, temperature (0.7 vs. 1.0), perspective shifts, and explicit self-debiasing, demonstrating robustness of the optimism/pessimism effect.

findings.title: Model Identity Dominates Language Effects
findings.detail: Variance decomposition shows 35.3% of Skew variance is attributable to model identity, while inter-language variance accounts for only 7.5% (1/4.7 of model variance), indicating model choice matters more than language.

findings.title: Differential Effects on Probability Coherence
findings.detail: Conjunction axiom violations are low (0–10%) and stable across languages, but dose-response monotonicity violations remain high (27–47%), suggesting alignment training improves some coherence axioms but not others.

contributions: Introduction of OptimismBench, a novel benchmark using inverted pairs to detect directional bias in LLM probability judgments without ground-truth probabilities.
Empirical demonstration that most commercial and open-source LLMs exhibit significant optimism bias, with only Anthropic’s frontier models showing pessimism.
Controlled base-versus-chat experiments establishing post-training alignment as a causal factor influencing bias direction in a family-specific manner.
Cross-lingual evaluation showing model identity dominates language effects on directional bias, with inter-model variance 4.7× inter-language variance.
Release of a large multilingual dataset (3,870 items across 10 languages) for auditing directional bias in LLMs.
limitations: The family-direction claim relies on limited matched pairs (Qwen 5/5, Llama 4/4) and single-pair pilots (Gemma-2-2b, Mistral-Small-24B), limiting statistical power within families.
Skew measures internal asymmetry against the complementarity axiom rather than deviation from human judgment; no matched human baseline is provided.
Cross-lingual evaluation includes languages with English system prompts, introducing a known confound that may affect language variance estimates.
The study does not provide mechanistic causal models or equations explaining why alignment induces directional bias.
open_questions: How does directional bias in LLM probability judgments affect downstream decision-making and real-world applications?
Can alignment training be designed to mitigate optimism or pessimism bias without sacrificing helpfulness or safety?
What are the cognitive or architectural mechanisms by which post-training alignment shifts bias direction in different model families?
How do human probability judgments compare to LLM Skew scores on the same inverted-pair scenarios, and can human baselines guide bias correction?

papers.title: OmegaUse-OfficeVal: Benchmarking LLM Agents on Long-Horizon Office-Suite Tasks with Economic Grounding
papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents are increasingly expected to assist users in completing tasks. However, existing benchmarks provide limited support for evaluating whether agents can carry out office-suite workflows at a reasonable cost. We introduce OmegaUse-OfficeVal, a benchmark for evaluating LLM agents on long-horizon office-suite tasks with task-level economic grounding. The benchmark comprises 100 tasks derived from office-suite requests proposed by practitioners and adapted through a privacy-preserving process. On average, these tasks require 2.32 hours of human labor to complete. An important feature of the benchmark is that each task is paired with two economic signals: human labor time and task price proxy. These signals enable direct comparisons between human costs and LLM inference costs, as well as value-weighted evaluation. To support stable evaluation, we develop code-based verifiers from fine-grained rubrics. We evaluate several frontier LLMs together with a human baseline. Although all evaluated LLMs are substantially cheaper and faster than human workers, they have not yet approached human-level deliverable quality. The code and dataset are fully open-sourced, and more information is available on our project website: https://omegause-officeval.github.io.

summary.takeaway: OmegaUse-OfficeVal introduces a benchmark with 100 long-horizon office-suite tasks paired with economic signals to evaluate LLM agents on cost-quality-time trade-offs.
summary.problem: Existing benchmarks inadequately assess LLM agents’ ability to complete complex office-suite workflows with economic grounding reflecting human labor and market value.
summary.method: The benchmark combines practitioner-derived tasks, human labor time and task price proxies, and code-based verification from fine-grained rubrics to evaluate final deliverables.
summary.evidence: Evaluations show LLMs are substantially cheaper and faster than humans but have not reached human-level deliverable quality across diverse office-suite domains.
summary.limitations: Current LLMs exhibit uneven performance across domains and task types, and the benchmark lacks evidence on uniform capability and trajectory-level evaluation.
summary.why_for_you: This benchmark enables rigorous, economically grounded evaluation of LLM agents on realistic, long-horizon office tasks critical for trustworthy productivity AI.

signals.text: OmegaUse-OfficeVal tasks average 2.32 hours of human labor and include economic signals: human labor time and task price proxy, enabling value-weighted evaluation of LLM agents.
The benchmark employs a deterministic code-based verification protocol using expert-revised rubrics to evaluate final office deliverables rather than fixed execution trajectories.
Experimental results reveal that although LLM agents are faster and cheaper, none have matched human-level quality, with performance varying significantly by domain and task type.

deep_dive.overview: OmegaUse-OfficeVal addresses the gap in evaluating LLM agents on complex, long-horizon office-suite workflows by introducing a benchmark of 100 tasks derived from real practitioner requests. Each task is annotated with two economic signals: human labor time and a task price proxy, the latter combining explicit market prices and expert estimates to reflect real-world value. The evaluation protocol uses code-based verification with fine-grained rubrics to assess final deliverables, allowing multiple valid workflows. This approach enables direct comparison of human and LLM costs and quality, including value-weighted metrics emphasizing tasks with higher labor or market value. Experiments with several frontier LLMs and human baselines show that while LLMs are substantially cheaper and faster, they have not yet achieved human-level deliverable quality, with performance varying across domains, output file types, and operation intents. This benchmark thus provides a comprehensive, economically grounded framework for assessing LLM agents’ practical utility in office automation.

methodology.title: Task Collection and Economic Annotation
methodology.detail: Tasks were collected from practitioner office-suite requests and adapted via a privacy-preserving process. Each task is annotated with human labor time measured in minutes and a task price proxy derived from explicit price signals for 20% of tasks and expert estimates aggregated through a consistency-based procedure for the remainder.

methodology.title: Task Price Proxy Estimation
methodology.detail: For tasks lacking explicit price data, three domain experts independently estimate task value based on occupational category, complexity, and typical compensation. Outlier estimates are discarded based on gap ratios, and the final proxy is the mean of consistent estimates, ensuring economic grounding and coverage.

methodology.title: Code-Based Verification Protocol
methodology.detail: Evaluation uses deterministic code-based verification of final output files against expert-revised rubrics with about 20 rubric items per task. This approach supports multiple valid workflows and focuses on deliverable quality rather than execution trajectory.

methodology.title: Value-Weighted Scoring Metrics
methodology.detail: Three scoring metrics are used: raw task score, time-weighted score (weighting by human labor time), and price-weighted score (weighting by task price proxy). These metrics enable nuanced evaluation of agent performance considering economic value and human effort.

mechanism.title: Economic Grounding via Hybrid Price Proxy
mechanism.detail: The task price proxy mechanism combines explicit market prices with expert estimates to provide a comprehensive economic value annotation. The consistency-based aggregation discards outliers by comparing adjacent gaps among expert estimates, preserving real-world grounding while mitigating extreme values.

mechanism.title: Code-Based Verification Mechanism
mechanism.detail: The verification mechanism evaluates final deliverables using deterministic code that checks compliance with rubric criteria, allowing multiple valid workflows to produce acceptable outputs. This contrasts with trajectory-based or human-judged evaluation, providing stable and reproducible quality assessment.

experiments.title: Model and Human Baseline Evaluation
experiments.detail: Several frontier LLMs including GLM-5.2, Qwen3.7-Plus, DeepSeek-V4-Pro, Kimi K2.6, and MiniMax M3 were evaluated alongside human annotators on the 100-task benchmark using raw, time-weighted, and price-weighted scoring metrics.

experiments.title: Domain and Task-Type Performance Analysis
experiments.detail: Performance was analyzed across domains (e.g., Engineering, Business, Academic), output file types (Word, Excel, PPT), and operation intents (annotation, extraction, beautification). Results showed domain-specific strengths and weaknesses, with Excel and annotation tasks generally easier for LLMs.

findings.title: LLMs Are Cheaper and Faster but Lower Quality
findings.detail: All evaluated LLMs completed tasks at substantially lower cost and runtime than humans but did not reach human-level deliverable quality, confirming the benchmark’s challenge and the gap in current LLM capabilities.

findings.title: Performance Varies by Domain and Task Type
findings.detail: GLM-5.2 excelled in Engineering tasks, Qwen3.7-Plus in Business Operations, DeepSeek-V4-Pro in Academic Papers, and Kimi K2.6 in Other categories, indicating non-uniform LLM capabilities across office-suite workflows.

findings.title: Excel and Annotation Tasks Are More Tractable
findings.detail: Models performed better on Excel and Word tasks and on annotation and extraction operation intents, likely due to programmatic manipulability and clearer task specifications, whereas beautification tasks were more challenging.

contributions: Introduction of OmegaUse-OfficeVal, a benchmark with 100 long-horizon office-suite tasks annotated with human labor time and task price proxies.
Development of a deterministic code-based verification protocol using expert-revised rubrics for stable and reproducible evaluation of final deliverables.
Proposal of value-weighted scoring metrics that incorporate economic signals to assess LLM agent performance in terms of human labor and market value.
Comprehensive evaluation of multiple frontier LLMs and human baselines revealing cost-quality-time trade-offs and domain-specific performance variations.
limitations: The benchmark does not evaluate execution trajectories, focusing solely on final deliverable quality, which may overlook agent behavior nuances.
Economic annotations rely partly on expert estimates, which may introduce subjective bias despite consistency checks.
Current LLMs show uneven performance across domains and task types, indicating limited generalization and robustness.
The benchmark lacks evidence on how well LLM agents handle dynamic or interactive office workflows beyond static task completion.
open_questions: How can LLM agents be improved to achieve human-level deliverable quality across diverse long-horizon office-suite tasks?
What methods can better integrate economic grounding into agent training and decision-making to optimize cost-quality-time trade-offs?
How can evaluation protocols incorporate trajectory-level analysis to capture agent strategies and error recovery in office automation?
What approaches can enhance LLM robustness and generalization across heterogeneous office domains and task intents?

papers.title: \textsc{IH-Benchmark}: A Conflict-Centered Benchmark for Instruction-Hierarchy Robustness in LLM Applications
papers.abstract: When a language model receives conflicting instructions from different priority levels, which one does it actually follow? This question lies at the heart of reliable LLM deployment. Existing benchmarks answer this only partially, often focusing on a single hierarchy edge or adapting public datasets with limited tool-use coverage. We present IH-Benchmark, a conflict-centered benchmark for instruction-hierarchy robustness across direct system-user conflicts (S>U) and tool-mediated user-tool (U>T) conflicts. IH-Benchmark is built from a human-authored taxonomy of 44 constraint families across generic, health, finance, retail, and coding settings, and evaluates scenarios with a uniform binary pass/fail protocol combining a predicate DSL with category-scoped LLM judges. Across 37 evaluated models, hierarchy compliance ranges from 98.2% to 20.5%. We find that strong S>U compliance is not a reliable proxy for U>T robustness: several models preserve system constraints under direct user conflict but degrade sharply when conflicting instructions appear in tool outputs. Constraint hardening also reveals a split between models: some failures are largely fixed by stronger warnings, while others persist across all strictness levels. Finally, the most revealing failures are often subtle rather than overtly dangerous; models resist unauthorized purchases or bulk ticket closure more reliably than injected disclaimers or small factual distortions. These results suggest that instruction-hierarchy robustness is not a single capability, but a set of behaviors that must be evaluated across conflict surfaces, constraint types, and attack presentations.

summary.takeaway: Instruction-hierarchy robustness in LLMs is a multifaceted capability that varies significantly across conflict surfaces, constraint types, and models, with strong system-user compliance not guaranteeing robustness against user-tool conflicts.
summary.problem: Existing benchmarks inadequately evaluate LLMs' ability to follow conflicting instructions across multiple hierarchy levels, especially in agentic settings involving tool-mediated conflicts.
summary.method: IH-Benchmark (IH-B) is a procedurally generated benchmark with 2,336 scenarios across 44 constraint families, evaluating instruction-hierarchy robustness on system-user (S ≻ U) and user-tool (U ≻ T) conflicts using a binary pass/fail protocol with predicate DSL and LLM judges.
summary.evidence: Evaluation of 37 model variants shows compliance rates ranging from 98.2% to 20.5%, with models often robust on S ≻ U conflicts but significantly less so on U ≻ T conflicts, and varying performance across constraint types and strictness levels.
summary.limitations: IH-B focuses on bounded single-task scenarios and selected domains, lacking coverage of longer multi-turn interactions and broader domain diversity, with most constraint families hand-authored and not exhaustive.
summary.why_for_you: IH-B provides a comprehensive, conflict-centered evaluation framework critical for assessing and improving trustworthy LLM behavior in hierarchical instruction-following, especially in complex agentic and tool-using deployments.

signals.text: Across 37 evaluated LLM variants, instruction-hierarchy compliance varies widely from 98.2% to 20.5%, demonstrating that robustness is highly model-dependent and not uniform across hierarchy conflict surfaces.

IH-B uses a uniform binary pass/fail evaluation combining a predicate domain-specific language (DSL) with category-scoped LLM judges to systematically assess compliance with 44 human-authored constraint families across system-user and user-tool conflict tracks.

Models that maintain strong compliance in direct system-user conflicts (S ≻ U) often degrade sharply in user-tool conflicts (U ≻ T), indicating that robustness in one conflict surface is not a reliable proxy for overall instruction-hierarchy robustness.

deep_dive.overview: The paper addresses the critical challenge of instruction-hierarchy robustness in large language models, focusing on how models resolve conflicting instructions from different priority levels, such as system prompts, user inputs, and tool outputs. Existing benchmarks inadequately cover this problem, often focusing on a single hierarchy edge or adapting datasets without agentic tool-use scenarios. IH-Benchmark (IH-B) introduces a comprehensive, procedurally generated suite of 2,336 executable scenarios spanning 44 constraint families across generic and domain-specific settings. It evaluates two conflict tracks: system prompt versus user prompt (S ≻ U) and user input versus tool output (U ≻ T), using a binary pass/fail protocol with predicate DSL and LLM judges. The evaluation of 37 models reveals substantial variability in hierarchy compliance, with strong S ≻ U robustness not reliably predicting U ≻ T robustness. Compliance also varies by constraint type, instruction explicitness, and conflict phrasing, suggesting no single general mechanism for hierarchy conflict resolution. These findings highlight instruction-hierarchy robustness as a set of behaviors requiring multi-dimensional evaluation, informing safer and more reliable LLM deployment.

methodology.title: Scenario Generation
methodology.detail: IH-B procedurally generates 2,336 executable scenarios from a human-authored taxonomy of 44 constraint families spanning generic, health, finance, retail, and coding domains. Scenarios are organized into two tracks: system prompt versus user prompt (S ≻ U) and user input versus tool output (U ≻ T), enabling targeted evaluation of instruction conflicts across hierarchy levels.

methodology.title: Evaluation Protocol
methodology.detail: A uniform binary pass/fail protocol is employed, combining a predicate domain-specific language (DSL) to specify constraint compliance and category-scoped LLM judges to assess model outputs. This approach standardizes evaluation across diverse scenarios and constraint types.

methodology.title: Model Evaluation Setup
methodology.detail: 37 model variants were evaluated using LiteLLM, routing inference through APIs from OpenAI, Amazon Bedrock, xAI, and TogetherAI, with some self-hosted models served via vLLM on AWS EC2. Each scenario was executed once per model to measure hierarchy compliance.

methodology.title: Constraint Hardening
methodology.detail: The benchmark includes varying strictness levels (L1-L3) for constraints, enabling analysis of model robustness under increasing constraint severity and revealing differences in model failure modes and sensitivity to warnings.

methodology.title: Agentic and Tool-Mediated Evaluation
methodology.detail: IH-B integrates stateful agent simulators to evaluate hierarchy-following behavior in static, tool-mediated, and agentic settings, capturing realistic multi-turn and tool interaction dynamics within bounded single-task scenarios.

mechanism.title: Instruction Hierarchy Conflict Resolution
mechanism.detail: No explicit mechanistic or causal model is provided; the paper empirically demonstrates that instruction-hierarchy robustness is not governed by a single general mechanism but is a composite of behaviors varying by conflict surface, constraint type, and instruction phrasing.

experiments.title: Model Compliance Evaluation
experiments.detail: 37 LLM variants, including Claude Opus 4.6, GPT 5.4, Gemma 4 31B, and Llama 4 Scout 17B, were evaluated on IH-B's 2,336 scenarios. Compliance rates ranged from 98.2% to 20.5%, with detailed breakdowns by track (S ≻ U and U ≻ T), domain, and constraint strictness levels.

experiments.title: Constraint Strictness Ablation
experiments.detail: Compliance was measured across three constraint strictness levels (L1-L3), revealing that some models improve significantly with stronger warnings, while others exhibit persistent failures regardless of strictness.

experiments.title: Cross-Track Robustness Analysis
experiments.detail: The study compared model performance on system-user conflicts versus user-tool conflicts, finding that strong S ≻ U compliance does not reliably predict U ≻ T robustness, highlighting the need for multi-surface evaluation.

experiments.title: Domain-Specific Performance
experiments.detail: Performance varied across domains such as health, finance, retail, and coding, with some constraint families showing higher compliance and others revealing subtle failure modes like injected disclaimers or factual distortions.

findings.title: Wide Variability in Hierarchy Compliance
findings.detail: Instruction-hierarchy compliance across 37 models ranged from 98.2% to 20.5%, demonstrating significant variability in model robustness to conflicting instructions.

findings.title: S ≻ U Robustness Does Not Predict U ≻ T Robustness
findings.detail: Models that maintain system constraints under direct user conflict often degrade sharply when conflicting instructions appear in tool outputs, indicating distinct robustness challenges across conflict surfaces.

findings.title: Constraint Hardening Reveals Model Splits
findings.detail: Some models' failures are largely mitigated by stronger warnings (higher strictness), while others persist across all strictness levels, indicating heterogeneous failure modes.

findings.title: Subtle Failures More Revealing Than Overt Ones
findings.detail: Models resist overtly dangerous instructions like unauthorized purchases more reliably than subtle injected disclaimers or small factual distortions, suggesting nuanced vulnerabilities.

findings.title: No Single General Mechanism for Hierarchy Resolution
findings.detail: Compliance rates vary by constraint type, instruction explicitness, and conflict phrasing, indicating that current LLMs lack a unified approach to resolving instruction hierarchy conflicts.

contributions: Introduction of IH-B, a procedurally created benchmark with 2,336 scenarios covering system-user and user-tool instruction hierarchy conflicts across 44 constraint families.
Development of a unified evaluation framework combining predicate DSL and category-scoped LLM judges for binary pass/fail assessment of hierarchy compliance.
Comprehensive evaluation of 37 LLM variants demonstrating non-uniform instruction-hierarchy robustness across models, conflict surfaces, and constraint types.
Release of the IH-B benchmark corpus, agent simulators, and evaluation harness to facilitate future research on instruction-hierarchy robustness.
Empirical evidence that instruction-hierarchy robustness is a composite of behaviors requiring multi-dimensional evaluation rather than a single capability.
limitations: IH-B focuses on bounded single-task scenarios and does not cover longer multi-turn interactions where user instructions, memory, or tool state accumulate.
The benchmark covers a selected set of domains with asymmetry across tracks, limiting generalizability to broader domains and richer interaction types.
Most constraint families (35/44) were hand-authored by the authors, with the remainder suggested and filtered by GPT-5.3, so coverage is not exhaustive.
The evaluation executes each scenario once per model, which may limit statistical robustness of compliance measurements.
open_questions: How can instruction-hierarchy robustness be extended and evaluated in longer multi-turn, memory-augmented, and dynamic agentic interactions?
What architectural or training modifications can enable LLMs to develop a unified mechanism for resolving instruction hierarchy conflicts across diverse surfaces?
How do different types of constraints and instruction phrasings influence model robustness, and can adaptive prompting or fine-tuning improve generalization?
What are effective defenses against subtle instruction-hierarchy failures such as injected disclaimers or factual distortions that current models struggle to resist?

papers.title: Runtime Uncertainty Monitoring for LLM-Based Multi-Agent Systems Using Bayesian Networks
papers.abstract: This paper investigates how multi-agent systems (MAS)-based on large language models (LLMs) can support actuarial risk modelling, with a particular focus on uncertainty quantification. Actuarial workflows represent a high-stakes decision-support setting where unreliable outputs may lead to incorrect risk assessment, unfair pricing, and regulatory non-compliance. To address uncertainty introduced by the probabilistic nature of LLMs and dependencies between agents, a multi-agent framework is proposed in which specialised agents perform data preparation, modelling, review, and explanation tasks under a central hub. The main contribution is a novel approach to uncertainty propagation using token-level log-probabilities and a Bayesian Network. Importantly, log probabilities are not treated as direct probabilities of correctness or task success. Instead, length-normalised log-probability summaries are transformed into calibrated task-level confidence estimates before incorporation into the Bayesian Network. Results show that the framework reproduces baseline actuarial performance while providing additional insight into workflow stability and runtime uncertainty propagation.
papers.comment: This paper got accepted for Ninth International Workshop on Artificial Intelligence Safety Engineering (WAISE 2026): https://www.waise.org/

summary.takeaway: A novel runtime uncertainty-monitoring framework for LLM-based multi-agent actuarial systems uses calibrated token-level log-probabilities combined with a Bayesian Network to propagate and interpret uncertainty across workflow stages.
summary.problem: Uncertainty and error propagation in LLM-based multi-agent actuarial workflows risk incorrect risk assessment, unfair pricing, and regulatory non-compliance due to lack of transparency and error traceability.
summary.method: The framework employs specialized agents coordinated by a central hub, transforming length-normalized token log-probabilities into calibrated confidence estimates incorporated into a Bayesian Network modeling dependencies between agents and workflow stages.
summary.evidence: Results demonstrate that the multi-agent system reproduces baseline actuarial performance while providing additional insights into workflow stability and runtime uncertainty propagation, with effectiveness varying by LLM backend.
summary.limitations: The Bayesian Network abstracts workflow dependencies without modeling execution sequence, task priority, iterative revisions, or feedback loops, limiting dynamic uncertainty representation.
summary.why_for_you: This approach offers a structured, interpretable uncertainty quantification method for trustworthy LLM-based multi-agent systems in high-stakes actuarial risk modeling, addressing transparency and safety concerns.

signals.text: Calibrated length-normalized token-level log-probabilities are transformed into task-level confidence estimates, enabling uncertainty quantification that does not treat log probabilities as direct correctness probabilities.

A centralized multi-agent system architecture with specialized agents for data preparation, modeling, reviewing, and explanation is coordinated via a central hub that manages workflow oversight and error handling.

The Bayesian Network explicitly models dependencies between agent outputs as nodes and edges, allowing structured uncertainty propagation and identification of weak workflow points requiring human review.

deep_dive.overview: This paper addresses the challenge of uncertainty quantification and error propagation in LLM-based multi-agent systems applied to actuarial risk modeling, a high-stakes domain requiring transparency and reliability. The authors propose a centralized multi-agent framework where specialized agents perform distinct actuarial tasks coordinated by a central hub. The key innovation lies in leveraging token-level log-probabilities from LLM outputs, which are length-normalized and calibrated into task-level confidence scores. These confidence estimates feed into a Bayesian Network that models dependencies between agents and workflow stages, enabling structured uncertainty propagation across the entire workflow rather than isolated agent assessments. Experimental results show that this approach maintains baseline actuarial performance while providing additional insights into workflow stability and runtime uncertainty behavior. The framework supports multiple open-source LLM backends, revealing backend-dependent differences in error detection and uncertainty dynamics. Limitations include the Bayesian Network's static abstraction of workflow dependencies without modeling iterative revisions or feedback loops. Overall, the work contributes a novel, interpretable runtime uncertainty monitoring mechanism tailored for trustworthy LLM-based actuarial multi-agent systems.

methodology.title: Multi-Agent System Architecture
methodology.detail: A centralized star topology coordinates four specialized agents—Data Preparation, Modelling, Reviewing, and Explanation—via a Central Hub that routes tasks and manages workflow oversight, avoiding direct agent-to-agent communication to enable controlled error handling and revision.

methodology.title: Token-Level Log-Probability Extraction and Calibration
methodology.detail: Autoregressive LLM outputs generate token-level log-probabilities which are length-normalized and transformed into calibrated task-level confidence estimates, avoiding naive interpretation of log-probabilities as direct correctness probabilities.

methodology.title: Bayesian Network for Uncertainty Propagation
methodology.detail: A Bayesian Network models dependencies between agent outputs as nodes and edges, incorporating calibrated confidence estimates as evidence to propagate uncertainty through the workflow and identify weak points.

methodology.title: Concept Alignment and Fairness Assessment
methodology.detail: The Explanation Agent evaluates internal beliefs using Testing with Concept Activation Vectors and assesses fairness via group-level comparisons of predicted versus observed outcomes on sensitive attributes such as age and population density.

methodology.title: LLM Backend Integration
methodology.detail: The framework supports three open-source decoder-only transformer models—Llama 2 7B, Llama 3.1 8B, and Qwen2.5 7B—selected for local execution efficiency, enabling evaluation of backend-dependent uncertainty and error detection behavior.

mechanism.title: Uncertainty Propagation via Bayesian Network
mechanism.detail: The Bayesian Network explicitly encodes dependencies between agent decisions as nodes and edges, allowing structured propagation of calibrated confidence estimates derived from token-level log-probabilities across workflow stages. This enables runtime monitoring of uncertainty accumulation and identification of unsafe workflow states. No explicit equations or causal models beyond the Bayesian Network structure are provided.

experiments.title: Actuarial Workflow Performance Evaluation
experiments.detail: The multi-agent system was evaluated on actuarial risk modeling tasks, reproducing baseline performance while providing additional uncertainty insights. The evaluation involved comparing outputs across three LLM backends (Llama 2 7B, Llama 3.1 8B, Qwen2.5 7B) using metrics related to error detection, adaptability, and uncertainty behavior.

experiments.title: Uncertainty Distribution Analysis
experiments.detail: Uncertainty outcomes from test scenarios were compared between original and perturbed datasets using the Qwen backend, illustrating the framework's ability to detect distributional shifts and runtime uncertainty variations.

findings.title: Calibrated Log-Probability Confidence Enables Uncertainty Quantification
findings.detail: Transforming length-normalized token log-probabilities into calibrated confidence estimates allows meaningful uncertainty quantification that avoids misinterpretation of raw log-probabilities as correctness probabilities.

findings.title: Bayesian Network Captures Workflow Dependencies and Uncertainty Propagation
findings.detail: Modeling agent outputs and their dependencies as a Bayesian Network provides structured uncertainty propagation, enabling identification of weak workflow points and unsafe states requiring human intervention.

findings.title: Multi-Agent System Maintains Baseline Actuarial Performance
findings.detail: The MAS reproduces baseline actuarial modeling accuracy while adding runtime uncertainty insights, demonstrating practical viability in high-stakes insurance workflows.

findings.title: LLM Backend Choice Affects Uncertainty and Error Detection
findings.detail: Differences in error detection, adaptability, and uncertainty behavior were observed across the three LLM backends, indicating backend-dependent effectiveness of the uncertainty monitoring framework.

contributions: A novel uncertainty propagation approach combining calibrated token-level log-probabilities with a Bayesian Network in LLM-based multi-agent actuarial workflows.
A centralized multi-agent system architecture with specialized agents and a central hub enabling controlled workflow oversight and error handling.
Integration of concept alignment and fairness assessments within the Explanation Agent to support transparency and regulatory compliance.
Empirical demonstration that the framework reproduces baseline actuarial performance while providing additional runtime uncertainty insights.
Public release of Python implementation, datasets, and evaluation notebooks to support reproducibility.
limitations: The Bayesian Network abstracts workflow dependencies as a directed acyclic graph without modeling execution sequence, task priority, iterative revisions, or feedback loops.
The framework currently does not distinguish intrinsic versus extrinsic uncertainty, limiting granularity of uncertainty source identification.
Effectiveness depends on the selected LLM backend, with observed variability in error detection and uncertainty behavior.
No explicit modeling of temporal dynamics or iterative repair cycles; dynamic Bayesian Networks are proposed as future work.
open_questions: How can dynamic Bayesian Networks be integrated to capture temporal behavior and iterative repair cycles in multi-agent workflows?
What methods can effectively distinguish intrinsic from extrinsic uncertainty within LLM-based multi-agent systems?
How can the framework be extended to explicitly model execution sequence, task priority, and feedback loops for more accurate uncertainty propagation?
What are the implications of LLM backend variability on uncertainty quantification robustness and how can backend selection be optimized?

papers.title: Sharpness-Aware Minimization and Muon: Robustness under the Spectral Norm
papers.abstract: Sharpness-Aware Minimization (SAM) aims to improve generalization by encouraging insensitivity to small, worst-case parameter perturbations. However, the notion of a "small" perturbation is inherently geometry-dependent: while existing SAM variants have explored a wide range of choices, a clear perspective on which geometries are most effective in practice remains elusive. Recent work on matrix-aware optimization, particularly the Muon optimizer, suggests that respecting the matrix structure of hidden-layer weights can lead to strong empirical performance. Motivated by this, we study matrix-aware geometry in both stages of SAM: we introduce a layerwise spectral inner perturbation for matrix-valued hidden-layer parameters and combine it with either AdamW/SGDW or Muon in the outer update. Across ImageNet-1K experiments on ViT-Small/16 and ResNet-50, we find that the combination of a spectral inner step with a Muon outer step performs consistently strongly, achieving the best validation accuracy on both models among the evaluated methods.

summary.takeaway: Combining a spectral norm-based inner perturbation with the Muon optimizer as the outer update in Sharpness-Aware Minimization (SAM) yields superior validation accuracy on ImageNet-1K for ViT-Small/16 and ResNet-50.
summary.problem: Existing SAM variants lack a clear understanding of which perturbation geometries most effectively improve generalization, especially regarding matrix-aware spectral norms.
summary.method: The paper introduces a layerwise spectral inner perturbation for matrix-valued parameters combined with either AdamW/SGDW or Muon optimizers in the outer step to study spectral geometry effects in SAM.
summary.evidence: ImageNet-1K experiments show that spectral inner perturbations paired with Muon outperform Euclidean perturbations and AdamW outer steps, achieving up to 80.23% top-1 accuracy on ViT-Small/16.
summary.limitations: The study does not provide a differentiable selection for the spectral perturbation map and relies on stop-gradient approximations, limiting theoretical analysis of second-order effects.
summary.why_for_you: This work advances understanding of geometry-aware adversarial perturbations in SAM and demonstrates the practical benefits of spectral norm-based optimization for robust and generalizable LLM training.

signals.text: Spectral inner perturbations amplify the benefits of the Muon outer optimizer, achieving a 5.28 percentage point improvement in validation accuracy on ViT-Small/16 compared to 4.45 points with AdamW.

The method applies a layerwise spectral norm-based inner maximization step to find worst-case perturbations respecting matrix structure, combined with Muon's matrix-aware outer update that uses Newton-Schulz iterations for spectral normalization.

CIFAR-100 diagnostics reveal that Muon maintains higher effective rank in weight matrices and features, enabling larger perturbation radii and stronger regularization, while excessive radii reduce rank and degrade validation accuracy.

deep_dive.overview: The paper addresses the challenge of selecting effective perturbation geometries in Sharpness-Aware Minimization (SAM) by investigating spectral norm-based perturbations that respect the matrix structure of neural network weights. Motivated by the success of the Muon optimizer, which incorporates spectral geometry in the outer update, the authors propose combining a layerwise spectral inner perturbation with Muon or AdamW/SGDW outer optimizers. They formulate a norm-agnostic SAM framework using Fréchet differentials and dual norms to define adversarial perturbations under spectral norms. Empirical evaluation on ImageNet-1K with ViT-Small/16 and ResNet-50 shows that spectral inner steps paired with Muon yield the highest validation accuracy, outperforming Euclidean perturbations and AdamW outer steps. Additional diagnostics on CIFAR-100 demonstrate that Muon preserves higher effective rank in weights and features, supporting stronger regularization via larger perturbation radii. The work highlights the interaction between inner and outer geometries and establishes spectral geometry as a promising direction for robust optimization in deep learning.

methodology.title: Norm-agnostic SAM formulation
methodology.detail: The authors generalize SAM by defining the inner perturbation step as a maximization over a unit ball of an arbitrary norm, using the Fréchet differential DL(θ) and its dual norm ∥DL(θ)∥in,* to characterize the worst-case perturbation ε*. This allows replacing the Euclidean norm with spectral norms for matrix-valued parameters.

methodology.title: Spectral inner perturbation
methodology.detail: They introduce a layerwise spectral norm inner step that computes adversarial perturbations respecting the matrix structure of hidden-layer weights. This involves orthogonalized gradient ascent constrained by the spectral norm unit ball, approximated via iterative methods.

methodology.title: Outer update with Muon optimizer
methodology.detail: The outer step uses the Muon optimizer, which applies spectral norm-aware updates to matrix-valued parameters using Newton-Schulz iterations for spectral normalization, while non-matrix parameters are updated by AdamW or SGDW, enabling hybrid parameter routing.

methodology.title: Experimental protocol
methodology.detail: Experiments train ViT-Small/16 for 300 epochs and ResNet-50 for 120 epochs on ImageNet-1K, tuning learning rates and perturbation radii per method. Evaluation includes Top-1 accuracy, ImageNet-ReaL, and ImageNet-R benchmarks, with multiple random seeds for robustness.

mechanism.title: First-order adversarial perturbation via dual norm
mechanism.detail: The mechanism defines the inner maximization in SAM as finding ε* maximizing the linearized loss increase DL(θ)[ε] subject to ∥ε∥in ≤ 1, where ∥·∥in is a chosen norm (spectral norm for matrices). The dual norm ∥DL(θ)∥in,* quantifies the worst-case directional derivative, guiding the perturbation.

mechanism.title: Stop-gradient approximation
mechanism.detail: Due to non-differentiability and computational cost of the maximizer map ε*(θ), the method uses a stop-gradient approximation, evaluating the loss at θ + ρε* but ignoring the derivative of ε* with respect to θ, simplifying gradient computation during training.

experiments.title: ImageNet-1K classification with ViT-Small/16 and ResNet-50
experiments.detail: The authors evaluate SAM variants with Euclidean and spectral inner steps combined with AdamW/SGDW or Muon outer optimizers. Training uses large batch sizes, cosine learning rate schedules, and standard augmentations excluding Mixup and RandAugment to isolate optimization effects.

experiments.title: Out-of-distribution robustness on ImageNet-R
experiments.detail: Models are evaluated on ImageNet-R, a 30k-image artistic rendition dataset, to assess generalization beyond the training distribution, showing spectral SAM with Muon achieves top performance, though differences are not statistically significant across seeds.

experiments.title: CIFAR-100 diagnostic experiments
experiments.detail: Additional experiments on CIFAR-100 measure effective rank of weight matrices and features, and sharpness via projected gradient ascent at fixed radii, revealing that Muon maintains higher rank and that larger perturbation radii reduce sharpness and generalization gap.

findings.title: Spectral inner step benefits depend on outer optimizer
findings.detail: Spectral inner perturbations improve validation accuracy substantially only when paired with the Muon outer optimizer, achieving 80.23% top-1 accuracy on ViT-Small/16, outperforming Euclidean inner steps and AdamW outer steps.

findings.title: Muon optimizer maintains higher effective rank
findings.detail: CIFAR-100 diagnostics show Muon-based outer updates keep weight and feature effective ranks higher than AdamW-based variants, supporting stronger regularization and enabling larger perturbation radii without loss of representation capacity.

findings.title: Spectral SAM variants achieve lower training accuracy
findings.detail: Spectral inner step variants reach lower training accuracy than Euclidean counterparts, suggesting that spectral geometry imposes a harsher penalty on memorization, potentially improving generalization.

contributions: Formulation of a norm-agnostic SAM framework using Fréchet differentials and dual norms to incorporate spectral geometry.
Introduction of a layerwise spectral norm inner perturbation step respecting matrix structure in SAM.
Integration of the Muon optimizer as a spectral norm-aware outer update in SAM.
Empirical demonstration that spectral inner perturbations combined with Muon yield state-of-the-art validation accuracy on ImageNet-1K for ViT-Small/16 and ResNet-50.
Diagnostic analysis linking Muon's maintenance of high effective rank to improved robustness and generalization.
limitations: The spectral perturbation map ε*(θ) is non-differentiable and the method uses a stop-gradient approximation, limiting theoretical understanding of second-order effects.
The study focuses on vision models and does not evaluate on large language models despite Muon's relevance there.
Out-of-distribution improvements on ImageNet-R are not statistically significant across seeds, indicating limited evidence for robustness beyond standard validation.
The method requires tuning perturbation radii and hyperparameters separately for each SAM variant, which may limit practical applicability.
open_questions: How can differentiable spectral perturbation maps be constructed to enable exact gradient computation in spectral SAM?
What are the effects of spectral SAM variants on large language models and other non-vision architectures?
Can the interaction between inner and outer geometries be theoretically characterized to guide optimizer design?
How does spectral SAM affect adversarial robustness and calibration beyond standard accuracy metrics?

papers.title: Forecasting Trajectory-Level Safety Risks in Black-Box Multi-Turn Interactions
papers.abstract: As large language models (LLMs) evolve from standalone assistants into autonomous agents, ensuring their safety requires shifting beyond pointwise risk assessment to understand how risks emerge and unfold over long-horizon trajectories. In multi-turn interactions, malicious intent can be decomposed across seemingly harmless turns and gradually reconstructed through interaction trajectories, eventually resulting in safety failures. Existing safeguards remain largely reactive, detecting manifested violations while lacking the ability to predict latent risk evolution and enable preemptive prevention. To address this limitation, we propose Recast, a safety risk forecasting framework that advances LLM safeguarding beyond turn-level violation detection to trajectory-level risk prediction. Recast first retrieves risk-relevant evidence from both short-term dialogue progression and long-term historical context via a dual-scale trajectory view. It then models compositional risk evolution by capturing the current risk configuration and its temporal dynamics. Finally, a causal temporal encoder learns latent risk evolution patterns and predicts the distribution of future risk emergence turns. Extensive experiments across 7 risk categories show that Recast predicts 88.3% of future safety failures with an average lead time of 2.41 turns, while maintaining a false alarm rate of 12.3%, showcasing the effectiveness of trajectory-level forecasting in identifying emerging risks before safety violations occur.

summary.takeaway: Recast effectively forecasts trajectory-level safety risks in multi-turn interactions, achieving high predictive accuracy.
summary.problem: Existing safety measures are reactive and fail to predict latent risks in multi-turn interactions.
summary.method: Recast retrieves risk-relevant evidence and models risk evolution to forecast future safety failures.
summary.evidence: Recast predicts 88.3% of future safety failures with an average lead time of 2.41 turns and a false alarm rate of 12.3%.
summary.limitations: The study does not address the performance of Recast across all potential risk categories.
summary.why_for_you: Understanding Recast's trajectory-level forecasting can enhance the safety of LLMs in autonomous applications.

signals.text: Recast achieves a negative log-likelihood of 0.45 and a mean absolute error of 0.31 for first-risk emergence time forecasting, demonstrating its predictive capabilities.
The framework employs a dual-scale trajectory view to retrieve risk-relevant evidence from both short-term dialogue progression and long-term historical context.
Recast maintains a false alarm rate of 12.3% while achieving an early warning rate of 88.3%, indicating its effectiveness in proactive risk management.

deep_dive.overview: The research addresses the challenge of predicting safety risks in multi-turn interactions of LLMs, proposing Recast as a proactive forecasting framework. Unlike existing methods that react to safety violations, Recast anticipates risks by modeling the evolution of interaction trajectories. The framework retrieves relevant evidence and captures temporal dynamics, achieving significant predictive accuracy, as evidenced by its ability to forecast 88.3% of future safety failures with a lead time of 2.41 turns.

methodology.title: Risk-relevant historical evidence retrieval
methodology.detail: Recast captures both short-term and long-term contextual evidence to inform risk assessments, enhancing the model's understanding of evolving interactions.

methodology.title: Compositional risk state and transition modeling
methodology.detail: The framework constructs a structured risk state from retrieved evidence and models its temporal evolution, allowing for dynamic risk assessment.

methodology.title: Future risk distribution forecasting
methodology.detail: A causal temporal encoder is employed to learn latent risk evolution patterns, predicting the distribution of future risk emergence across interaction turns.

mechanism.title: Causal temporal encoding
mechanism.detail: Recast utilizes a causal temporal encoder to learn patterns of risk evolution, enabling the prediction of future safety violations based on past interactions.

experiments.title: Dataset construction
experiments.detail: The study constructs a dataset of 10,000 trajectories, balancing harmful and benign samples across 7 risk categories to train and evaluate Recast.

experiments.title: Evaluation metrics
experiments.detail: Recast is evaluated using negative log-likelihood (NLL), expected mean absolute error (Expected-MAE), early warning rate (EWR), and false alarm rate (FAR) to measure its forecasting capabilities.

experiments.title: Comparison with baselines
experiments.detail: Recast is compared against multiple safeguard baselines, demonstrating a reduction in attack success rates from 71.5% to 45.9%, showcasing its effectiveness.

findings.title: High predictive accuracy
findings.detail: Recast predicts 88.3% of future safety failures, indicating its strong capability in forecasting risks before they manifest.

findings.title: Effective early warning
findings.detail: The framework achieves an average lead time of 2.41 turns, allowing for timely interventions in multi-turn interactions.

findings.title: Low false alarm rate
findings.detail: Recast maintains a false alarm rate of 12.3%, demonstrating its reliability in distinguishing between benign and harmful interactions.

contributions: Introduces Recast, a novel framework for trajectory-level safety risk forecasting in LLMs.
Demonstrates the importance of proactive risk assessment in multi-turn interactions.
Provides empirical evidence of Recast's effectiveness across multiple risk categories.
limitations: The performance of Recast across all potential risk categories is not fully explored.
The study does not address the scalability of Recast in real-world applications.
open_questions: How can Recast be adapted to handle emerging risk categories not covered in the current study?
What are the implications of Recast's predictions on the design of future LLM safety protocols?

papers.title: ToxScreen: Detecting Whether an LLM Has Been Poisoned
papers.abstract: As large language models (LLMs) are deployed in high-stakes domains, adversaries may poison training data to implant backdoors: hidden triggers that covertly manipulate model behavior at inference time. We ask whether a defender can recover such a trigger under realistic affordances, namely white-box access to the weights and knowledge of the behavior of concern, but no training data, no trusted reference model, no knowledge of the trigger, and no certainty that the model is poisoned. To evaluate whether a defender can recover such a trigger under realistic settings, we release ToxScreen, a benchmark of roughly 800 backdoored models spanning attack objectives, trigger mechanisms, poisoning rates, model scales, and backdoor training mechanisms. We also assert that the backdoors are high-quality: they achieve high attack success rates, generalize to unseen harmful inputs, and preserve clean-task performance. Scoring recovery of the planted trigger, we find that gradient-based prompt optimization fails in recovery, whereas a token look-up that ranks candidates by attack-success rate recovers the trigger wherever the backdoor is effective. To understand this more, we study the relationship between attack behaviors and the weights of an LLM. We find a phenomenon whereby backdoors operate via different mechanistic strategies than jailbreaks, allowing defenders to filter jailbreaks. Finally, no method reliably surfaces every backdoor, but a broadly jailbreakable model is itself anomalous, a useful signal even when the exact trigger is not recovered. We release all models and evaluation code

summary.takeaway: ToxScreen enables detection and partial recovery of backdoor triggers in LLMs using a novel token look-up method and a coupling statistic derived from model weights without access to training data or clean models.
summary.problem: Detecting and recovering backdoor triggers in large language models under realistic conditions where defenders have white-box access to model weights but no training data, no trusted reference model, and no prior knowledge of the trigger.
summary.method: ToxScreen measures the coupling between input triggers and model parameters via a second-order gradient statistic (σ1) and ranks candidate tokens by their ability to suppress this coupling and maximize attack success rate to recover triggers.
summary.evidence: Experiments on a benchmark of roughly 800 backdoored models show that gradient-based prompt optimization fails to recover triggers, whereas token look-up ranking by attack-success rate reliably recovers triggers when backdoors are effective, supported by pruning studies showing backdoors are often localized.
summary.limitations: No method reliably surfaces every backdoor, and some backdoors, such as sentiment steering, are distributed and resilient to pruning, limiting detection and ablation effectiveness.
summary.why_for_you: This work provides a comprehensive benchmark and a novel white-box detection method that operates without training data or clean models, addressing a critical gap in realistic backdoor defense for LLMs.

signals.text: The coupling statistic σ1, derived from the mixed second derivative of a behavior readout with respect to model parameters and input, reveals a dominant singular direction corresponding to the backdoor trigger, enabling detection without explicit trigger knowledge.

The token look-up defense evaluates ∼24,000 candidate tokens by injecting each at the trigger position in held-out prompts and ranks them by attack success rate, successfully recovering planted triggers across diverse backdoor mechanisms.

Pruning experiments demonstrate that refusal-suppression backdoors are encoded in sparse, localized circuits that degrade faster than general capabilities under structured pruning, whereas sentiment steering backdoors are distributed and persist or amplify under pruning.

deep_dive.overview: This paper addresses the challenge of detecting and recovering backdoor triggers implanted in large language models under realistic defender affordances: white-box access to model weights and knowledge of the attack objective, but no access to training data, clean reference models, or trigger information. The authors introduce ToxScreen, a benchmark of approximately 800 backdoored LLMs spanning various attack objectives, trigger mechanisms, poisoning rates, and model scales. They propose a novel detection method based on measuring the coupling between input tokens and model parameters via a second-order gradient statistic (σ1), which captures how triggers reroute gradients along a dominant direction. Complementing this, a token look-up approach ranks candidate tokens by their ability to suppress this coupling and maximize attack success rate, enabling trigger recovery. Experiments show that gradient-based prompt optimization fails to recover triggers, while token look-up succeeds wherever backdoors are effective. Pruning studies reveal that some backdoors, like refusal suppression, are localized and can be ablated with minimal impact on general capabilities, whereas others, like sentiment steering, are distributed and resilient. The work also distinguishes backdoor mechanisms from jailbreaks, providing a signal to filter false positives. Despite no method reliably surfacing all backdoors, the presence of broadly jailbreakable models itself signals anomalies. The authors release all models and code to facilitate further research.

methodology.title: Measuring Attack Behaviors
methodology.detail: The behavior readout B(θ, x) is computed as the inner product between the model's residual stream at a specific layer and position and a unit vector representing the target behavior direction (e.g., refusal or sentiment). This scalar is differentiable with respect to both model parameters θ and input x, enabling gradient-based analysis restricted to the last k transformer blocks.

methodology.title: Token-to-Parameter Coupling Statistic (σ1)
methodology.detail: The coupling M is defined as the mixed second derivative ∂²B/∂θ∂x, mapping input perturbations to changes in the parameter gradient of B. The operator norm σ1 (largest singular value) of M is computed via power iteration without explicit matrix formation, serving as a detection statistic indicating the presence of a trigger that reroutes gradients along a dominant input direction.

methodology.title: Suppression Ratio Scoring
methodology.detail: For each candidate token c, the suppression ratio ρ(c) = σ1(x_c)/σ1(x_∅) compares the coupling statistic when the token is injected versus a trigger-free input. Tokens with ρ(c) ≤ 0.70 are flagged as suppressors, indicating potential triggers that suppress the refusal mechanism and enable backdoor activation.

methodology.title: Token Look-up Attack Success Rate Ranking
methodology.detail: A candidate pool of approximately 24,000 vocabulary tokens plus the planted trigger is evaluated by injecting each token at the trained trigger position in about 150 held-out prompts. Candidates are ranked by their attack success rate (ASR), with recovery declared when a candidate's ASR significantly exceeds baseline, indicating successful trigger identification.

methodology.title: Pruning Strategies for Backdoor Localization
methodology.detail: Five pruning strategies (structured removal of attention heads, MLP layers, global and layer-wise unstructured magnitude pruning, and random pruning) are applied at varying sparsity levels to backdoored models. Attack success rate and general capability (MMLU) are measured to assess whether backdoors are localized and can be preferentially ablated.

mechanism.title: Backdoor Trigger Gradient Rerouting
mechanism.detail: Backdoor triggers operate by rerouting the gradient of the behavior readout B along a single dominant input direction, captured by the largest singular value of the mixed second derivative matrix M = ∂²B/∂θ∂x. This rerouting suppresses normal refusal mechanisms, enabling covert manipulation of model behavior. No explicit equations beyond those defining σ1 and ρ are provided.

experiments.title: Token Look-up Recovery Evaluation
experiments.detail: Evaluated on roughly 800 backdoored models fine-tuned from six instruction-tuned LLMs including Llama-3.2-1B and Qwen3-4B, the token look-up method injects ∼24,000 candidate tokens at trigger positions in held-out prompts and ranks them by attack success rate. Recovery is successful when the planted trigger ranks highest, demonstrating reliable trigger identification without training data.

experiments.title: Gradient-based Prompt Optimization Baseline
experiments.detail: Gradient-based prompt optimization methods, which search input space to maximize backdoor activation, were tested but failed to recover planted triggers across the benchmark, highlighting the superiority of the token look-up approach.

experiments.title: Pruning Ablation Studies
experiments.detail: Five pruning strategies at sparsity levels 0%, 10%, 50%, and 90% were applied to backdoored models. For refusal suppression backdoors, structured pruning at 50% sparsity reduced attack success rate from ~21% to ~7-10% while retaining ~75% of MMLU accuracy, indicating localized backdoors. For sentiment steering backdoors, pruning did not preferentially ablate attacks and sometimes increased attack success rate even as general capability collapsed.

experiments.title: General Capability and Safety Evaluation
experiments.detail: Backdoored models were evaluated on ARC, TruthfulQA, HellaSwag, and Winogrande benchmarks to assess impact on general capabilities. Attack success was scored using fixed judges including HarmBench Llama-213B for anti-refusal compliance and Llama-3-8B-Instruct for sentiment steering, ensuring consistent and objective evaluation.

findings.title: Token Look-up Recovers Triggers Reliably
findings.detail: The token look-up method successfully recovers planted triggers across diverse backdoor configurations, outperforming gradient-based prompt optimization which fails to recover triggers, demonstrating the effectiveness of ranking candidates by attack success rate.

findings.title: Backdoors Exhibit Distinct Mechanistic Signatures
findings.detail: Backdoors operate via different mechanistic strategies than jailbreaks, allowing defenders to distinguish and filter jailbreak behaviors from backdoor triggers using the coupling statistic and suppression ratio.

findings.title: Refusal Suppression Backdoors Are Localized
findings.detail: Pruning experiments show refusal suppression backdoors degrade faster than general capabilities under structured pruning, supporting the hypothesis that these backdoors are encoded in sparse, localized circuits.

findings.title: Sentiment Steering Backdoors Are Distributed and Resilient
findings.detail: Sentiment steering backdoors persist or even amplify under pruning, with attack success rates increasing to 61-81% at 90% sparsity while general capability collapses, indicating distributed encoding that resists ablation.

findings.title: No Method Surfaces All Backdoors Reliably
findings.detail: Despite advances, no detection method reliably identifies every backdoor, but broadly jailbreakable models themselves are anomalous, providing a useful signal even when exact triggers are not recovered.

contributions: Release of ToxScreen, a benchmark of ~800 backdoored LLMs spanning diverse attack objectives, mechanisms, and scales.
Introduction of a novel coupling statistic (σ1) based on second-order gradients to detect backdoor triggers without training data or clean models.
Development of a token look-up method that ranks candidate tokens by attack success rate to reliably recover planted triggers.
Empirical demonstration that refusal suppression backdoors are localized and can be preferentially ablated via pruning, while sentiment steering backdoors are distributed and resilient.
Identification of mechanistic differences between backdoors and jailbreaks, enabling filtering of false positives.
limitations: No detection method reliably surfaces every backdoor, limiting comprehensive defense.
Sentiment steering backdoors are distributed and resilient to pruning, complicating ablation and detection.
The approach requires white-box access to model weights, which may not always be available in deployment scenarios.
The benchmark and methods focus on instruction-tuned LLMs and may not generalize to all model architectures or training regimes.
open_questions: How can detection methods be improved to reliably surface all types of backdoors, including distributed ones like sentiment steering?
Can the coupling statistic and token look-up approach be adapted for black-box or limited-access scenarios?
What are the mechanistic underpinnings that differentiate backdoors from jailbreaks at a finer granularity?
How do backdoor detection and ablation methods generalize across different LLM architectures and training datasets?
